evidence.label: Uniform Matrix Hitting Points in Every Positive Characteristic
One Rational Matrix Hitting Point for Noncommutative Formulas
Polynomial Hitting Lists for Noncommutative Rational Formulas

headline: One fixed set of matrices exposes every nonzero small formula whose variables do not commute.
scope: The results cover formulas of bounded size, not circuits that reuse shared pieces; the division result is over the rationals.
plain: Some expressions look like zero for ordinary numbers but not for matrices, where multiplication order matters. These papers build matrices in advance that catch every nonzero formula up to a given size. One paper proves that a single tuple of fraction matrices works over every characteristic-zero field (Lean proof listed). A second proves that a short list handles formulas with division (Lean proof listed). A third claims to prove that one tuple works in each prime characteristic too.
doesNot: This does not cover general circuits that reuse shared pieces, and it does not make evaluating an unknown formula fast.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Ran Raz and Amir Shpilka, a deterministic test that reads the formula
scorecard.significanceWhy: It replaces quasipolynomial-size hitting sets with polynomial ones for formulas, with and without division.

explanation:
Take the expression x·y − y·x. Put in any two ordinary numbers and you get 0, because 3·5 equals 5·3. Now put in two small grids of numbers called matrices. Let X have rows (0, 1) and (0, 0). Let Y have rows (0, 0) and (1, 0). Then X·Y has rows (1, 0) and (0, 0). But Y·X has rows (0, 0) and (0, 1). Their difference has rows (1, 0) and (0, −1), which is not zero. Matrices can expose an expression that ordinary numbers make look like zero.

Matrices do this because their order of multiplication matters. Variables whose order matters are called noncommutative. A noncommutative formula builds an expression from variables and numbers using only addition and multiplication, arranged as a tree. Its size counts every piece of the tree, numbers and variables included. The basic question is identity testing: does a given formula compute zero once everything is multiplied out?

These papers ask for the hardest version of that test. You may not look inside the formula. You may only plug matrices in and see the result. Worse, you must choose the matrices in advance, knowing only the number of variables and a size limit. A hitting point is one fixed choice that gives a nonzero answer for every nonzero formula within those limits. A hitting list is a short list of choices where at least one works.

The obstacle is that a small formula can hide a huge expression. Multiply x₁ + x₂ by itself 10 times, keeping the order. The formula has 39 pieces. Multiplied out, it has 1024 different words, such as x₁x₂x₂x₁… in every order. A fixed set of matrices must keep all of them from cancelling, for every formula, without seeing any of them.

Earlier work left a gap. Ran Raz and Amir Shpilka gave a fast exact test in 2005, but it needs to read the formula. Andrej Bogdanov and Hoeteck Wee gave a test that only plugs in matrices, but it relies on random choices. In 2013, Michael Forbes and Amir Shpilka built fixed hitting sets without randomness. Their sets have quasipolynomial size, which grows faster than any fixed power of the formula size. In 2026, Foram Lakhani and Partha Mukhopadhyay built one fixed matrix tuple for sparse expressions, those with few words. A small formula can have very many words, as the example shows.

The first paper proves that one fixed tuple is enough over the rational numbers (fractions). For n variables and size limit s, the paper also claims at most 2ns² rows. It claims a build time that grows like a fixed power of n and s. The same tuple works over every number system where no whole number other than 0 equals zero. For the example, n = 2 and s = 39, so 6084 rows suffice. The idea is to turn each word into its own distinct infinite list of numbers. A small formula's list cannot begin with too many zeros, so a finite window of the list is enough.

The second Lean-checked paper handles division. A rational formula may also invert a matrix, which only works when that matrix is invertible. It proves a polynomial-size list of fraction-valued matrix tuples for such formulas with fraction constants. Every nonzero formula with some defined matrix value gets a defined, invertible value on some listed tuple. This holds however deeply inverses nest and however large the constants are. Earlier hitting sets of V. Arvind, Abhranil Chatterjee and Partha Mukhopadhyay had quasipolynomial size.

The third paper moves to characteristic p, for a prime p. There, adding p copies of 1 gives 0. The fraction method breaks there. It divides by whole numbers, and dividing by p is impossible there. Slopes also fail: when p = 2, the slope of z² is 2z, which is 0. The paper replaces slopes with a shift that multiplies z by a new symbol. It claims to prove that one tuple works in each characteristic p, including p = 2. Its matrices have on the order of n³s⁶ rows, more than in the fraction case. It is built in time polynomial in n, s and the number of digits of p.

These results do not say formulas can be evaluated quickly. The time bounds cover building the matrices, not plugging in an unknown formula. The first paper asserts no bound for circuits that reuse shared pieces. How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked two statements. One is that a single fraction-valued tuple hits every nonzero formula of size at most s. That Lean statement does not include the 2ns² row bound or the time bound. The other is the full hitting-list theorem for formulas with division, including its polynomial bounds. The characteristic p paper is outside the Lean scope note. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean has checked the single-tuple hitting property and the division hitting-list theorem. The single tuple's size and time bounds and the whole characteristic p paper are not in that check. No specialist review has been published.

glossary.meaning: A square grid of numbers that can be added and multiplied; the order of multiplication matters.
Describes variables where x times y need not equal y times x.
An expression built as a tree of additions and multiplications, with no shared pieces.
Deciding whether an expression computes zero once everything is multiplied out.
One fixed choice of matrices that gives a nonzero answer for every nonzero formula in a class.
Growing faster than any fixed power of the input size, but much slower than exponential growth.
The number of copies of 1 that add to 0 in a number system; 0 if none do.
A computer program that checks mathematical proofs step by step.
